239. ὑπείροχος: higher. Lg

240. 〈σὺν ἑῇ ναίεσκε δάμαρτι:〉 The author of the Naupactica (fr. 4 Kinkel) calls her Eurylyte, Dionysius of Miletus (32 fr. 1b Jacoby) calls her Hecate, mother of Medea and Circe, as has been said before (sch. 200a, b), Sophocles (fr. 344 Pearson) calls her Neaera, one of the Nereids, and Hesiod calls her Idyia (Theog. 958, 960): 'Aeetes, son of the sun that shines on mortals, married Idyia of the fair cheeks by the will of the gods.' Epimenides (3 B 13 Diels-Kranz) says that Aeetes was a Corinthian by birth, and says that his mother was Ephyra. Diophanes in the first book of his Pontic Histories (Diophanes fr. 1 M. IV 397) says that Antiope was the mother of Aeetes.

10 Διοφάνης: the author is identified by Ed. Schwartz, RE² V 1051
242-44. τὸν μὲν Καυκασίῃ: He says that Absyrtus was born before Medea from Asterodeia, daughter of Oceanus and Tethys.
14 here the scholiast wrongly transferred the parentage of Idyia to Asterodeia
249. 〈μετιοῦσαν: λείπει〉 εἶδον. Sm

255. ἔκτοθι πᾶσαι: instead of ἐκτός, so that it may signify motion to a place.
17 ἐκτός in L : ἔκτοσε in P
257. ὑψοῦ χάρματι χεῖρας: It should be ὑψόσε; for ὑψοῦ indicates rest in a place, while ὑψόσε indicates motion to a place. Homer (A 486) 'ὑψοῦ ἐπὶ ψαμάθοις'.
17 251. Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) ἀμφεπονεῖτο: διέτριβεν. III 251.
260-61a. οὐκ ἄρ’ ἐμέλλετ’ ἀκηδείῃ μελιπόν〈τες〉: Though you left me without care, nevertheless you were not destined to go far; fate has made you turn back.
b. τηλόθι: Here too it should be τηλόσε. Lg (P)
262. ἔκποθεν ἄτης: from some harm. LgP
264. 〈στυγεράς:〉 hated. Sm
265. Ὀρχομενοῖο: Hellanicus (4 fr. 126 Jacoby) also says that Athamas dwelt in Orchomenus. L.
267. ἑήν: instead of ὑμετέραν. Lg (P)
275. πολιοῖο: transparent. Lg (P)
276-77a. τετρηχώς: roughened. LgP

b. The oestrus differs from the gadfly. For the gadfly is born from wood, while the oestrus is born from small creatures that float on rivers. τέλλεται is formed by removal of the sigma, instead of στέλλεται.
7 added by W

281a. ὀξέα δενδίλλων: glancing sharply and nodding with the eyes. Homer (I 180) used the word for turning the eyes, but others say it means to nod with the eyes while turning the face aside, as Apollodorus (244 fr. 242 Jacoby) also says; Sophocles (fr. 1039 Pearson) used the word for looking around.
